content: Tipepidine, also known by its International Nonproprietary Name (INN), is a synthetic, non-opioid medication classified as an antitussive (cough suppressant) and expectorant. It belongs to the thiambutene chemical class. The drug functions by inhibiting G protein-coupled inwardly-rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs). Tipepidine was first discovered in the 1950s and subsequently developed in Japan in 1959. It is typically administered in the form of hibenzate or citrate salts. The standard recommended dosage is 20 mg, taken every 4 to 6 hours. Adverse effects associated with tipepidine, particularly in cases of overdose, may include drowsiness, vertigo, delirium, disorientation, confusion, and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness. In recent years, tipepidine has attracted attention for its potential applications in psychiatry. It is currently being studied for its therapeutic effects in conditions such as depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The drug’s mechanism of action involves the inhibition of GIRK channels, which leads to an increase in dopamine levels within the nucleus accumbens. Notably, this dopaminergic effect does not result in heightened locomotor activity or behavioral sensitization similar to that caused by methamphetamine. This specific action is thought to contribute, at least in part, to the antidepressant-like effects observed in preclinical studies involving rodents.
